answers.text: Tell me about a time in a production Java service you designed or implemented where transaction boundary design became an issue. Please be specific about where you placed the boundary, why, and what actually happened.
answers.answer: At the neobank, our core-ledger service does double-entry bookkeeping: every transfer between accounts must write a debit and a credit row atomically, and for years we wrapped that write together with a call to our notification service inside one Spring transaction, since it was simple and worked fine while we had under 50,000 accounts. As we grew past 400,000 accounts, our midnight standing-order batch, which processes maybe 60,000 transfers in a ten-minute window, started showing serious lock contention on the account_balances table -- I traced it with Postgres's pg_locks view and found transactions were held open for 200-400ms because the notification call inside them was slow and occasionally retried. My decision was to shrink the transaction to only the debit and credit write, which must stay atomic together for correctness, and move the notification into an outbox table written in the same transaction, drained by a separate poller. Lock hold time dropped to under 15ms. The failure that followed: under a later 5x traffic spike, the outbox poller itself became a bottleneck and fell eight minutes behind, so customers got transfer notifications late; I fixed that by sharding the poller by account-id range instead of running it single-threaded.
answers.says: Names a concrete transaction-boundary problem in a production Java service they were responsible for (e.g., lock contention on a long transaction, an external API call left inside a transaction, inconsistency from an isolation level), describes where they moved the boundary and the grounds for that decision (measurements, a real incident, data-consistency requirements), and covers the outcome or the fix for a failure, with numbers and time frames. Beyond just ‘we did it as a team,’ their own judgment and hands-on work are clear, and they can explain a design failure in their own words.

answers.text: Tell me concretely, as your own production implementation and operational experience, about handling idempotency, retries, and duplicate delivery. Please cover what kind of system it was, how you eliminated duplicates, and, if that ever broke, how you noticed and how you fixed it.
answers.answer: Every transaction that hits core-ledger carries an idempotency key made of a client-generated request ID plus our internal transaction type, enforced with a unique constraint on a transactions table, and any retried request -- from a client timeout, a mobile app resend, or our own internal retry after a downstream timeout -- gets the original result returned instead of a second debit or credit. This broke for real about two years ago: a partner payment provider we integrate with started retrying webhooks with exponential backoff after a change on our side slowed our webhook handler's acknowledgment past their 3-second timeout, and during a four-hour window before we noticed, roughly 1,200 webhook retries came in. Our idempotency key was built from the provider's own event ID, which we assumed was unique, but it turned out their retries sometimes carried a regenerated event ID after their fifth retry attempt, so 40 of those 1,200 slipped through as duplicate credits totaling about €6,800. We caught it the next morning through our automated reconciliation job comparing our ledger totals against the provider's settlement file. We corrected the 40 duplicates with reversing debit entries, not deletions, and fixed the root cause by keying on the provider's original transaction reference instead of their per-attempt event ID, since that field stayed stable across all of their retries.
answers.says: Names the concrete mechanism they implemented and operated (idempotency-key design, store choice, duplicate-delivery detection, reconciliation mechanism), why they chose that design, and the process of noticing and recovering when an incident or duplication actually occurred, with numbers (scale, count, time taken) and time frames. If it was an experience of resolving a consistency mismatch, they can also describe the root-cause triage and the grounds for correcting it with a new journal entry or record rather than an overwrite.

answers.text: Tell me about your experience and thinking on migrating from Java to Rust. If you have production Rust experience, tell me its scope; if not, tell me how you think you could realistically learn the differences from Java — ownership, lifetimes, async runtimes. Also tell me your thinking on how to decide a service boundary.
answers.answer: I do have production Rust experience. About three years ago I built and now help run our risk-engine service, which scores every incoming transaction for fraud risk in real time before core-ledger commits it. We chose Rust because the scoring model needs to run in under 10ms at p99 including feature lookups, and our early Java prototype of the same logic was sitting at 45-60ms at p99, mostly from GC pauses interrupting a latency-sensitive hot path we couldn't tolerate pausing. The Rust service uses tokio for the async runtime and tonic for gRPC, talking to core-ledger over a synchronous-feeling request-response call that core-ledger blocks on before committing a transaction. In production it now handles about 300 transactions per second at peak, with p99 around 6ms. The failure I'd point to: about a year in, we had a memory leak from a cache we weren't evicting properly, which grew slowly enough that it took two weeks to show up as pod restarts from OOM kills, and I found it with heaptrack rather than anything obvious in our metrics. My view on migration generally is the same principle that got us here: cut a boundary where there's a real, measured problem, not because the language is more fun to write.
answers.says: If they have production Rust experience, they describe which part of production it was (e.g., why latency became an issue, how they cut the boundary with Java, the measurement results), with numbers and time frames, and can describe failures too. If they lack production experience, they explain the concrete differences from Java in ownership, lifetimes, and async runtimes in their own words, and describe a realistic learning plan (what they have already written, read, or been studying). In addition, they state a view that fits our approach — deciding a boundary and migrating while measuring, rather than a full rewrite — together with their own grounds for it.

answers.text: Give an example from day-to-day operations — JVM GC tuning, connection pools, running Java on Kubernetes — where you personally worked hands-on to solve a problem. Tell me what you measured, what you changed, and what changed as a result.
answers.answer: Operationally, the biggest problem I've owned was GC pauses on our transaction-processing pods once we moved to Kubernetes and started running four replicas under real load. We were on the G1 collector with default settings, and once daily transaction volume passed around two million, we started seeing GC pauses of 800ms to 1.2 seconds roughly every ten minutes, which was enough to trip our p99 latency SLO of 300ms for transfer confirmation. I pulled GC logs with -Xlog:gc and found young-generation collections were the problem, not full GCs, because our heap was undersized relative to allocation rate -- we were allocating a lot of short-lived DTOs per transaction. I increased the young-gen size, from roughly 512MB to 1.5GB of a 4GB heap, and switched our JSON serialization to reuse buffers instead of allocating a new one per request, which cut allocation rate significantly. Pause frequency dropped from every ten minutes to roughly every forty, and p99 pause length came down to under 150ms. It took two rounds to get there -- my first attempt was just raising overall heap size, which didn't help pause frequency and increased full-GC pause length when it did happen, so I reverted that part and focused on generation sizing instead.
answers.says: Names a concrete operational problem in a Java service they operated (e.g., latency degradation from GC pauses, connection pool exhaustion, an OOM on Kubernetes), and describes the measurement tools used, the numbers obtained, the changes tried, the results (with figures), and, if the first fix missed, the failure and the retry. Can explain the triage process in their own words, with grounds for the decisions rather than a list of tool names.

answers.text: If you were to move part of the ledger write path to Rust, where would you start, where would you place the boundary with Java, and what would you measure before and after the migration to make that call? If you've cut out a language or service boundary before, please answer in light of that experience.
answers.answer: For our risk-engine boundary specifically, I placed it right before core-ledger commits a transaction: core-ledger calls out over gRPC with the transaction's features already assembled, gets back an allow/deny/review decision, and only then proceeds with its own commit. I kept the boundary narrow deliberately -- the Rust service owns scoring and nothing about the ledger's own consistency, so a bug in Rust can reject or approve a transaction but can never corrupt account balances, which live entirely on the Java side. Before migrating, we measured the Java prototype's p99 (45-60ms) and its GC-pause correlation with scoring latency spikes; after the Rust version shipped, we tracked p99 (down to 6ms), error rate, and, for about six weeks, ran the Java and Rust scorers side by side on shadow traffic to compare decisions before letting Rust be authoritative. About 0.3% of transactions disagreed during that shadow period, which we tracked down to a floating-point rounding difference in one feature calculation between the two implementations, and we didn't cut over fully until that gap closed to zero. If I were doing the ledger write path itself rather than a scoring sidecar, I'd apply the same shadow-and-measure approach, but I'd be more conservative about the boundary, since correctness there is much less forgiving of any gap.
answers.says: Concretely describes how to choose a migration target (measuring hot paths, starting with lower-risk parts), how to place the boundary (the shape of the interface, how to keep data consistent, coexisting with Java), and what metrics to watch before and after migration (latency, memory, correctness reconciliation), together with their own grounds for those decisions. If they've carved out a boundary before, they include the numbers, failures, and how they built agreement with the team. Fits our ‘decide the boundary before you rewrite’ approach, and can also describe how they resisted the temptation to do a full rewrite.

answers.text: In Rust code you've actually written — production or a personal project, either is fine — tell me a spot where you got stuck on ownership, lifetimes, or async, and how you resolved it. If you haven't written any yet, just say so.
answers.answer: In the risk-engine, the ownership problem that took me longest was around our feature cache: I wanted multiple tokio tasks to read from a shared HashMap of recent transaction features while one background task periodically evicted old entries, and my first instinct, coming from Java, was to reach for something like a mutex around the whole map, which worked but serialized every read behind the evictor, killing our latency target under load. I moved to a sharded structure -- effectively several smaller maps each behind their own RwLock, keyed by a hash of the customer ID -- so reads mostly don't contend with each other or with eviction on a different shard. The Send/Sync fight came later, when I tried to share a metrics-reporting closure across tasks that captured a non-Sync type from an early version of our metrics library; the compiler wouldn't let me spawn it across threads, and I spent a confused afternoon before realizing the library had a Sync-safe handle type I wasn't using, exposed under a different name than I expected. On async specifically, an early version of the gRPC handler accidentally held a lock across an .await point during a downstream call, which caused a deadlock under load that took me a day of tokio-console tracing to find, since it only showed up past a certain concurrency level.
answers.says: Names concretely what failed to compile in their own code (e.g., a borrow conflict, a lifetime annotation, a Send/Sync constraint, a tokio runtime boundary), how they fixed it, and how they came to understand the fix, in their own words. If it was production work, which part of production it was comes out concretely; if personal, what they built comes out concretely.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you shared a mistake or a delay early, and about your experience with on-call, handling inquiries, or mentoring juniors. For both, please be concrete about what you yourself did.
answers.answer: On sharing early: about a year ago I pushed a config change to the risk-engine's feature-lookup timeout that I thought was safe, and it quietly increased our false-decline rate by roughly 0.4 percentage points for eleven hours before a product manager noticed customer complaints ticking up. Once I traced it back to my change, I posted in our incident channel within fifteen minutes of confirming it, named it as my mistake specifically rather than 'a regression,' and we estimated the number of wrongly declined transactions -- about 340 -- so support could reach out proactively. On-call and mentoring: I've carried on-call for the risk-engine and core-ledger, combined, for about six years across two companies, one week in four currently, and I still take pages myself rather than routing everything to whoever's more junior. I mentor two engineers who joined in the last year, one of whom I'm walking through their first on-call rotation next month, shadowing with me first. I don't think of any of this as beneath the work of designing systems; the on-call load is exactly what tells me whether a design decision I made was actually a good one once it meets real traffic, so I'd trust my own design judgment less if I'd stopped carrying a pager.
answers.says: Can describe a concrete example of sharing their own mistake or delay before it got worse — what, when, to whom, how it was communicated, and what happened as a result. Also names a real example of taking on on-call rotation, inquiry handling, or mentoring juniors as their own job (duration, frequency, approach), and can describe never having thought of it as ‘not my real job.’ Both are told as their own actions, including experience of sharing within a blameless culture.

answers.text: Have you ever, while responding to an urgent incident, felt tempted to skip review or the normal deployment procedure? Tell me what you actually did, and what you think would need to be in place to justify a decision to skip a step.
answers.answer: During the OOM-restart incident, once I understood the leak but before I'd fully tested the LRU fix, I was tempted to skip our normal canary rollout and push straight to all pods, since restarts were getting more frequent and I wanted the bleeding to stop. What I actually did was resist that and stick to the procedure: I deployed to one canary pod first, watched its memory curve for about 40 minutes against my prediction, confirmed it was flat where the others were climbing, and only then rolled out to the rest, which added maybe an hour of that pod cycling through a few more restarts than if I'd gone straight to all of them. In hindsight I think that was the right call, because my LRU cap number was a guess, and if it had been wrong I'd have wanted to know that from one pod, not all of them at once. I have skipped procedure exactly once, years earlier at a previous job, during a payment outage, and in hindsight I don't think it was justified -- the outage wasn't getting worse, I was just impatient. The bar I hold myself to now: skip only if measurable harm is actively growing, not just present, and even then announce it and get at least one other set of eyes before deploying, not after.
answers.says: Names a concrete experience of being forced to choose between the procedure and an emergency, and describes what they actually did. If they skipped it, they describe the steps — announcing it beforehand, recording it afterward, and following up with the normal procedure once recovered — together with the criteria for that skip decision. If they didn't skip it, they describe why (not shipping a change they can't verify, money is not a test environment) and an alternative way to move quickly and safely without cutting the procedure. Either way, their own judgment and its outcome come through as a concrete example.

answers.text: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a team's technical decision. How did you voice the disagreement, how was it decided, and what did you do after the decision was made?
answers.answer: About four years ago, the team wanted to move core-ledger off Postgres onto a distributed database for horizontal scaling, arguing we'd hit a wall as account count grew. I disagreed, and spent a week benchmarking our actual write throughput against Postgres's documented limits, showing we were using about 8% of a single primary's write capacity even at peak, and that our real growth constraint was the midnight-batch lock contention I described earlier, not raw throughput. I presented that alongside a rough migration-cost estimate, and the team agreed to hold off on the database migration and instead invest in fixing the batch contention, which is the outbox change I made. I didn't quietly keep planning the distributed-database migration on the side; I dropped it entirely once the decision was made, and revisited it three years later, when account growth had actually caught up to a real throughput concern, at which point I was the one who reopened the conversation with new numbers rather than resisting it out of attachment to my earlier position. Separately, I've argued for and lost a case for rewriting a legacy batch-reporting job in Rust for speed, and once the team decided the reporting job wasn't worth the migration risk given how rarely it changes, I maintained it in Java without revisiting that.
answers.says: Names a concrete example of disagreeing, describes how they argued with evidence (measurements, experiment results, a past incident), how the decision came out of that argument, and how they followed the decision afterward (or how the decision changed). Can also describe not overturning it alone after the fact, or, if they nearly did, how they stopped themselves. If they've ever argued for a full rewrite out of technical preference, they can describe how they held that impulse in check.

answers.text: Have you ever felt tempted to use production data or balances to check that something worked? What did you actually do in that situation? When something can't be reproduced in a test environment, how do you go about verifying it?
answers.answer: Yes, particularly with the risk-engine's shadow-traffic comparison I described: the honest answer is that comparing real transaction decisions between Java and Rust implementations meant touching real transaction data, and I handled that by making the Rust scorer's decision purely advisory during the shadow period -- it computed a result and logged it, but core-ledger never acted on it, so there was no risk of the comparison itself affecting a real customer, even though the underlying data was live and real. For situations where I couldn't get away with even that, like verifying the interest-accrual idempotency fix under real concurrent load rather than staging's much lower traffic, I used a masked copy of a weekend's real transaction volume replayed against a staging environment scaled to match production concurrency, rather than testing against live accounts. I have, once, checked a single live account balance directly, during the interest-accrual incident, to confirm my hypothesis about the average overpayment before writing the correction script, and I posted the specific account ID I was checking in our incident channel along with why, rather than treating it as routine. I don't think occasional, announced, read-only checks against production are the same as using production as a general test environment, but I do try to keep the bar for doing even that fairly high.
answers.says: Names a concrete situation where they were tempted to check something in production, and describes the method they actually used (reproducing it on a masked copy, comparing via shadow execution, a read-only reconciliation, a canary), the grounds for that decision, and the cost it took. If they had no choice but to check in production, they can also describe how they announced it, recorded it, and limited the impact.

fit.says: The candidate is broadly aligned with most of the working principles, but shows a conditional attitude in some areas — for example, saying something to the effect of ‘in an emergency, you should fix it first even if it means skipping the procedure,’ without committing to announcing and recording that skip, or not speaking positively about on-call or support work. They could work here, but some coaching would be needed to bring them fully in line with the principles.
